title: Bombieri–Vinogradov for primes with a missing decimal digit
credit: QED original (archived Nov 2026, restored after re-review).
plain: Maynard proved there are infinitely many primes with no digit 7 in base 10, with the expected count. Show these primes are also well spread over arithmetic progressions, on average over all moduli up to a small power of x, as the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem says for all primes. Nath (arXiv:2108.09212) proved such a Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem at level x^{1/3−δ} for primes missing a digit in a sufficiently large base (roughly 10^632); the task is base 10, using Maynard's base-10 Fourier estimates.
math: Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of positive integers with no digit $7$ in base $10$, and for $(a,q)=1$ let $\pi_{\mathcal S}(x;q,a)=\#\{p\le x \text{ prime}: p\in\mathcal S,\ p\equiv a \ (q)\}$, $\pi_{\mathcal S}(x)=\pi_{\mathcal S}(x;1,0)$. Prove there is $\theta>0$ such that for every $A>0$: $\sum_{q\le x^{\theta},\,(q,10)=1}\ \max_{(a,q)=1}\big|\pi_{\mathcal S}(x;q,a)-\pi_{\mathcal S}(x)/\varphi(q)\big|\ll_A \pi_{\mathcal S}(x)(\log x)^{-A}$.
